Fig. 5 Phylogenetic tree of the SLC1 family. Fig. 6 Expression of excitatory amino acid transporters in neurons and astrocytes. Glutamate is released into the synaptic cleft and acts on AMPA and NMDA glutamate receptors, which are permeable to Na + and Ca 2+ , respectively, resulting in membrane depolarization and action potential generation. High affinity glutamate transporters regulate glutamate concentration and thus neurotransmission by removing the excitatory neurotransmitter from the synaptic cleft. Glutamate transporters are also essential for maintaining extracellular glutamate concentration below neurotoxic levels. The five high-affinity glutamate transporters (EAAT1 to 5) have distinct regional and cellular localizations. GLT1/EAAT2 ( SLC1A2 ) is mainly expressed in glia throughout the central nervous system and is responsible for 90% of the glutamate uptake. EAAC1/EAAT3 ( SLC1A1 ) is a postsynaptically localized neuronal glutamate transporter that is widely distributed throughout the central nervous system. The figure shows the glutamate-glutamine cycle, which helps maintain an adequate supply of the neurotransmitter glutamate in the central nervous system. Fig. 7 Phylogenetic tree of the SLC2 family. Fig. 8 The transport and metabolism of vitamin C and dehydroascorbic acid (DHA) in the human body. The vitamin C transporter SVCT1 ( SLC23A1 ) absorbs L-ascorbate (vitamin C) across the intestinal brush border membrane. How it leaves the epithelial cells is still unknown. There are two possible routes to the brain. 1) across the choroid plexus (blood-cerebrospinal fluid barrier) via the vitamin C transporter SVCT2 ( SLC23A2 ) located in the basolateral membrane and GLUT12 ( SLC2A12 ) located in the apical membrane of choroid plexus epithelial cells and then from the cerebrospinal fluid across the ependymal cell layer via unknown transporters; and 2) across the BBB as DHA via GLUT1/ SLC2A1 (not shown; see Fig. 33 ). Since DHA is present in blood at relatively low concentrations compared to vitamin C, the SVCT2 route via the choroid plexus appears to be the predominant pathway. In neurons, vitamin C is oxidized to DHA, which is released by GLUT3 ( SLC2A3 ). Astrocytes import DHA via GLUT1 and reduce it to vitamin C. The exit pathway of vitamin C from astrocytes is currently unknown. Neurons import vitamin C via SVCT2, closing the vitamin C recycling pathway. DHA is rapidly taken up by erythrocytes via the abundantly expressed glucose transporter GLUT1 ( SLC2A1 ). Intracellularly, DHA is reduced to vitamin C by glutathione, glutaredoxin or thioredoxin reductase, with the end result of replenishing plasma vitamin C levels. Fig. 10 Phylogenetic tree of the SLC4 family. Fig. 12 Kidney acid-base control via SLC4 bicarbonate transporters and SLC42 Rhesus glycoprotein ammonium transporters. The kidney contributes to acid-base homeostasis through the recovery of filtered bicarbonate in the proximal tubule. In the distal tubule, intercalated cells generate new bicarbonate, which is consumed by the titration of non-volatile acid. Proximal tubular acidosis results from dysfunction of the proximal tubule, where the majority of bicarbonate is reabsorbed. Intercalated cells are also involved in the excretion of ammonia/ammonium. Fig. 24 Phylogenetic tree of the SLC13 family. Fig. 25 Schematic model of the role of renal urea transporters in the urine concentrating mechanism. Urea is reabsorbed by UT-A1 and UT-A3 in the inner medullary collecting duct (CD) and accumulates in the medullary interstitium, while UT-B plays a role in countercurrent exchange between the descending vasa recta (DVR) and ascending vasa recta (AVR) to maintain medullary hypertonicity ( 9 ). Consistent with knockout data ( 10 ), UT-A2 contributes to urea accumulation in the medullary interstitium by reabsorption of urea in the descending thin limb (tDL), a process that requires active urea secretion in the proximal tubules (see orange arrows with question mark). However, the molecular nature of active urea secretion remains elusive, despite a hypothesized mechanism ( 25 ). Independent of urea, NaCl reabsorption and accumulation in the renal medulla via NKCC2 expressed in the thick ascending limb (TAL) is considered to play an important role in urine concentrating mechanisms by initiating hypertonicity in the inner medullary interstitium. Fig. 56 Roles of PTCH1 and DISP1 in the Hedgehog (HH) signaling pathway. SHH-producing cells secrete the sonic hedgehog (SHH) protein, a signaling molecule crucial for development and homeostasis (top part of the figure). The HH pathway plays a role in the development of many tissues during embryogenesis and has also been shown to function in self-renewing adult tissues ( 1 ). SHH-target cells (bottom part of the figure) respond to the SHH protein by activating downstream signaling pathways that lead to changes in gene expression and cellular behavior. These cells play crucial roles in embryonic development, tissue regeneration, and diseases, including cancer.
